title: Starting from nothing
hookLine: refugee Sikhs rebuilt lives in Delhi and East Punjab

lines: A CRATE ON A DELHI PAVEMENT.
cards: What do you sell when everything you owned is on the other side of a border? A few combs, some bars of soap, a row of pencils, laid out on a wooden crate turned upside down on a Delhi pavement.
Behind the crate, a man in a turban who, a few months earlier, owned land or a shop in a town that is now in Pakistan.
Stories like this are told in Punjabi families: a grandfather who sold things off a crate, a grandmother who sewed through the night, a camp of tents, a first rented room.
The refugees came into Delhi and East Punjab carrying what they could hold. Then they started again.

teach.b: First, the arrival. Families who had crossed the border lived in camps, in shelters, in the crowded homes of relatives. Land, shops and houses were gone.

Some had lost people too, and carried that along with the bundles. Second, the work. Sikh teaching sums up a life in three short instructions often traced to Guru Nanak: naam japo, kirat karo, vand chhako.

teach.h: KIRAT KARO: EARN BY HONEST WORK.
teach.b: Remember the Name, earn by honest work, share what you have. The middle one is kirat, honest labor. In the stories families tell of those years, it was the thing they could still hold on to when nothing else was left.
A crate became a stall, a stall a shop, a shop a living. Third, the Guru's measure. Early on this path you met Bhai Lalo, the carpenter of Saidpur.

Tradition says Guru Nanak ate Lalo's coarse bread, earned by his own hands, and turned down a rich man's feast. Not the one who had the most: the one who worked honestly and shared. Fourth, the sharing.
In the stories of those years, langar was cooked even in the camps, the free kitchen now feeding people who had nothing, sometimes cooked by people who had very little more.
Starting over and giving away turned out not to be opposites.
From nothing but hands, honest work, and a shared pot.

how: Sikhs speak of kirat karo, earning by honest work, alongside naam japo and vand chhako, and Punjabi families descended from Partition refugees retell how their elders rebuilt their lives.

o: honest work, earning a living by your own hands
a tax on land that refugee farmers had to pay
a vow of silence kept from dawn until noon

p: the carpenter whose plain bread the Guru ate

s: in the old story, Guru Nanak chose the rich man's feast
tradition says he ate the coarse bread of Lalo the carpenter, earned by honest work.
langar was cooked in the refugee camps
the free kitchen kept going, feeding people who had nothing.
kirat means a life of prayer apart from work
kirat is honest labor; it sits beside remembering the Name and sharing.

games.q: you've arrived in Delhi with a bundle and a family. your shop and land are gone. what do you do first?
o: go back across the border to look for what was lost.
set up a crate on the pavement and start selling.
sit in the camp and wait for the old life to return.
games.why: in the stories families tell, a crate became a stall, a stall a shop. kirat, honest work, was what they still had.

practice: Think of one thing you've wanted to start and haven't, because you didn't feel ready: a skill, a garden, a savings jar, a letter, an apology.
Don't plan the whole of it; find only the very first step, small enough for what you already have, and breathe in seeing your hands doing it, breathe out letting go of the perfect start.
If you pray, rest on Waheguru as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Kirat, honest work: kirat karo, earn by honest labor. The refugees of Partition rebuilding their lives in Delhi and East Punjab, with honest work and shared bread. Today's word.
